meta.section: §1-§2 (Sentence and clause; Canonical and non-canonical clauses)
meta.assumed_inputs: No highest-ID list was supplied; numbering starts at CLS-001. No Burton-Roberts index supplied, all mappings 'unverified'.

concepts.gloss: largest unit of syntax; occurs in sequence in texts
syntactic construction with subject and predicate in central cases; can be embedded
clause contained within a larger clause
sentence form made of coordinated clauses
mixed coordination of a noun phrase and a clause
basic clause construction: positive, declarative, active, main, non-coordinate
clause differing from a canonical counterpart on one or more dimensions
canonical clause differing only on one dimension
clause in which a subordinate clause is embedded
word (e.g. that, to) marking a clause as subordinate
word (e.g. and, or, but) marking coordination
position before the nucleus clause, e.g. for fronted wh- elements or auxiliaries

rules.statement: A sentence is the largest syntactic unit and sentences occur in sequence in a text without generally being contained in one another; a clause is a construction of subject plus predicate (in central cases) and can be embedded inside a larger one.
rules.condition: Applies when deciding whether a stretch of text is a sentence or a clause: it is a sentence only if it is one of the units occurring in succession in a text, and a clause if it has subject-predicate structure in the central cases; the same string can be a sentence in one text and merely part of a sentence in another.

correct.note: Standalone: both a sentence and a clause.

correct.text: Mara left early, but Jon stayed.

contrast.text: I heard that Mara left early.
contrast.note: 'Mara left early' is a clause here but not a sentence; it is only part of one.

rules.review_notes: Also records that relations between sentences in a discourse are outside the book's grammar (p. 44); not made a rule.

rules.concept: sentence has the form of a clause or clause-coordination
rules.statement: A sentence has either the form of a clause or the form of a coordination of clauses; 'clause', not 'sentence', is the syntactic category used in constituent-structure trees.
rules.condition: Applies when assigning a category to the top node of a constituent-structure analysis of a sentence: a sentence with one subject-predicate structure (with or without embedded clauses) is labelled clause; a sentence of coordinated clauses is labelled clause-coordination; the label 'sentence' is not used for syntactic categories.

correct.text: The dog barked, and the cat ran off.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Cambridge rejects 'sentence' as a syntactic category label; Burton-Roberts's usage not checked.

rules.review_notes: Reasons given on p. 45: (a) treating a coordination and its coordinate parts as one category fails for mixed coordinations; (b) it clashes with the everyday sense of 'sentence'. These are Cambridge's analytical arguments, not tested constraints.

rules.statement: A coordination belongs to a different category from its coordinate parts and is named by what it coordinates: clause-coordination, NP-coordination, or a mixed form such as NP/clause-coordination.
rules.condition: Applies to any coordinative construction: the whole is categorised as a coordination of the categories of its parts, and is not assigned the category of any single coordinate; mixed coordinations (e.g. a noun phrase joined to a clause) have a mixed label.

correct.text: You should ask [the price and whether we can pay by card].

rules.review_notes: Detailed treatment is in Ch. 15; this record covers only the Ch. 2 overview.

rules.statement: Cambridge treats the traditional simple/complex/compound trichotomy as conflating two independent dimensions, embedding and coordination, and so uses non-compound (clausal) vs compound instead, making little further use of simple vs complex.
rules.condition: Applies when classifying a sentence by clause structure: embedding (presence of a subordinate clause) and coordination (presence of coordinated clauses) are independent; a sentence can have both, one, or neither.

correct.text: I think Mara left, but Jon stayed.

rules.review_notes: Source is footnote 1, p. 45. Cambridge's stance on a traditional scheme; do not use it to flag 'errors'.

rules.statement: Canonical clauses are the basic constructions (positive, declarative, active, main, non-coordinate); non-canonical clauses differ from them along one or more of five dimensions: polarity, clause type, information packaging (e.g. passive), subordination, and coordination.
rules.condition: Applies when describing a clause: compare it with its canonical counterpart on each of five independent dimensions: polarity (negative), clause type (interrogative, exclamative, imperative), packaging (passive, preposing, existential, it-cleft), subordination (subordinate), coordination (coordinate); a clause may be non-canonical on several dimensions at once.

correct.text: Mara did not read the letter.
The letter was read by Mara.

rules.review_notes: Cambridge's five dimensions are in the numbered list on pp. 46-47. 'All canonical clauses are declarative' (p. 46) is encoded in the condition.

rules.concept: negative and interrogative counterparts: auxiliary do
rules.statement: When a canonical clause with no auxiliary verb is made negative or interrogative, the non-canonical form adds the semantically empty auxiliary do; interrogatives also invert subject and predicator.
rules.condition: Applies to the specific contrasts illustrated on p. 46 (a positive declarative clause without an auxiliary versus its negative or interrogative counterpart); the full conditions on do-support are given elsewhere in the book (Chs. 3, 9, 10), not here.

correct.text: Mara did not read the letter.

rules.review_notes: This overview only describes the pattern. Do not turn it into an error-detection rule from this source; extract the actual constraint from Chs. 3/9/10.

rules.statement: A subordinate clause is embedded in a matrix clause; subordination can repeat, so a matrix clause may itself be embedded in a larger one.
rules.condition: Applies when a clause is contained within another clause: the containing clause is the matrix clause for the contained subordinate clause; a subordinate clause may be marked by a subordinator (e.g. 'that') or consist of a VP with a subordinator 'to' with subject and object unexpressed.

correct.text: Mara said that Jon was ill.
correct.note: 'Jon was ill' is subordinate; the whole is its matrix clause.

correct.text: I think Mara said that Jon was ill.
correct.note: Recursive: matrix clause embedded in a larger one.

rules.review_notes: Cambridge notes subordinate clauses can differ from main clauses far more than by a subordinator alone (p. 47).

rules.statement: Non-canonical properties are independent, so one clause can be negative, interrogative, passive and subordinate at once, and its structure is described by its difference from canonical structure on each dimension separately.
rules.condition: Applies to any clause showing more than one non-canonical feature; each feature is analysed on its own dimension, and the counterpart for one feature retains the other features.

correct.text: I can't see why the window was not closed by Jon.

contrast.note: Active counterpart: 'Sue didn't write it' (still negative); positive counterpart: 'It was written by Sue' (still passive).

rules.statement: Not every non-canonical clause has a grammatically well-formed canonical counterpart, so process descriptions (passivisation, inversion) cannot be read as a derivation from a canonical clause.
rules.condition: Applies to non-canonical clauses whose construction is restricted to that form: negative clauses containing negative-polarity items such as 'any longer'; interrogatives containing 'yet'; passive-only 'say + infinitive'; existentials with no non-existential counterpart; subordinate clauses with no main-clause counterpart.

contrast.note: Positive counterpart of a negative: ill-formed in the intended sense (cf. p. 47 [3i]).
Declarative counterpart of an interrogative: ill-formed (cf. p. 47 [3ii]).

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.review_notes: The book shows ill-formed counterparts for illustration, but the constraints on negative-polarity 'any' and 'yet' belong to Ch. 9. Mark these 'contrast', not a testable rule, until Ch. 9 is processed. Cambridge's own example on p. 47 ('It had been for you') is grammatical under a different, referential interpretation.

rules.statement: Terms like subject-auxiliary inversion, passivisation and relativisation are convenient descriptive labels for how a non-canonical clause differs from a canonical one, and do not claim that speakers derive one clause from another.
rules.condition: Applies when interpreting process terminology in any chapter: such terms can always be restated in static terms (for example, 'the auxiliary comes before the subject, the reverse of canonical order'); the book is an informal descriptive grammar, not a generative one.

correct.note: Described as inversion; statically: auxiliary precedes subject.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Burton-Roberts may use derivational terminology; not checked.

rules.statement: In an interrogative subordinate clause such as 'what Liz bought', the fronted element is in the prenucleus position and the rest is the nucleus; the position it is understood to fill within the nucleus is shown by a gap co-indexed with it, rather than by relabelling the fronted element as the object.
rules.condition: Applies to clauses where an element before the subject is understood as filling a function (such as object) inside the nucleus clause, including across further embedding: the gap occupies that function in the clause of the verb it belongs to, not in the clause where the fronted element stands.

correct.note: 'what' is prenuclear and understood as object of 'bought'.

correct.text: I can't remember what Jon said Mara bought.

rules.review_notes: The tree diagrams are on pp. 48-50; trees were not examined as images for this pass.

rules.concept: no overt object after an object gap
rules.statement: When an element in the prenucleus is understood as the direct object of the verb in the nucleus, that object position is a gap and no overt direct object may follow the verb.
rules.condition: Applies to an interrogative clause (e.g. subordinate, introduced by an interrogative NP like 'what') whose prenuclear NP is understood as the direct object of a transitive verb in the nucleus.
rules.violation: An overt direct object appears after the verb whose object is already realised by the prenuclear interrogative element (e.g. 'what Mara bought a watch').

correct.text: She asked what Jon had broken.

incorrect.text: *I wonder what Mara bought a watch.
incorrect.note: Overt object duplicates the object already supplied by 'what'. Source: p. 49.

incorrect.text: *She asked what Jon had broken the vase.

rules.concept: subject-auxiliary inversion analysed with a gap
rules.statement: Subject-auxiliary inversion is analysed as a prenucleus (the auxiliary) plus a nucleus identical to the canonical clause except that the predicator position is a gap co-indexed with the fronted auxiliary, so the grammatical relations among subject, verb and complement stay the same as in the declarative.
rules.condition: Applies to main-clause interrogatives with inverted subject and auxiliary: the fronted auxiliary is in the prenucleus, the gap takes its place as predicator in the nucleus; wh-interrogatives therefore involve one prenucleus-plus-nucleus construction inside another.

correct.note: 'is' fronted; its predicator position is a gap.
Nucleus 'had Jon bought' functions inside the outer nucleus.
